inspected_context_lines.text: 4. Give only the bold noun, without an article: (a) the fruit of one **tree**; (b) the bird is in one **tree**; (c) several **trees** are in the dwelling; (d) the meaning of one **sign**; (e) several **signs** are in the sky; (f) the sound of the **water**; (g) the **waters** are in the sea; (h) several **evenings** have passed; (i) the **cattle** are in the dwelling. Label the forms. Explain the **w** in (c), and contrast the loss or retention of the middle stem vowel in (e) and (g).
1. You are speaking about yourself: “I was in the tree.” Then change only the time: “I am in the tree.”

4. You speak for yourself and one companion: “We two are in the sea.” Put this in the past, then restate the past sentence for a group of three that includes you. Explain which pronoun changes and why the verb's number does not.
5. Address two companions: “You two were in the dwelling.” Put this in the present, then restate the present sentence to address a group of three. Explain the choices of pronoun and verb.
| **ofer ðǣre nēowolnesse brādnesse** | **Ofer** means “over” and here requires a dative head. Apply the nested-genitive construction of §9 to identify the head and its dependent. |

12. Cook, *First Book*, §§160,164(a), pp.93–94 / PDF109–110; §166, p.95 / PDF111; §§168,172, pp.96–97 / PDF112–113. **Sealde** is printed in §117, p.72 / PDF88. The other supplied frames occur in the assigned Creation extract. Examples in §9 are new composition. Supplied finite forms do not introduce their full conjugations.

16. Cook, §81, pp.48–49 / PDF64–65, gives the personal-pronoun paradigms. The subject inventory selects **hēo** and **hīe**, with **ðū** following this unit's spelling convention. Ringe and Taylor, *The Development of Old English* (2014), §1.1.2, p.6 / preview PDF21, explicitly states that the dual pronouns take plural verbs. Fulk's Genesis 19 reading, p.38 / PDF50, uses ordinary second- and first-person plurals for the two angels, illustrating that plurals can include two. Only nominative subject use is introduced here.

17. Fulk, *An Introductory Grammar of Old English* (2020), glossary p.265 / PDF277, prints unpointed **cyn(n)**; §18, p.12 / PDF24, gives its **k** value. The stopped initial of **gærs** is a source-based inference: Wright and Wright, *Old English Grammar*, second edition (1914), §§314–315, p.156 / PDF176, classify **græs** with guttural **g** and describe its stopped initial outcome; §§66 note 4 and 345, pp.43,171 / PDF63,191, connect **gærs** with late r-metathesis. Compare Wright §85 note 1, p.47 / PDF67, for breaking before this metathesis, and Fulk §72, p.46 / PDF58, for palatalization before breaking. The learner needs only the supplied sound, not this historical derivation.

Locative **on** requires D in (a) and (d); the images are a G dependent in (b), and the likenesses a N subject in (c). The **-nes** nouns retain **e** and have doubled **ss** before their endings: **fæstness-**, **andlīcness-**, **gelīcness-**. **Gegaderungum** adds **-um** directly to **gegaderung-**. Identical **-a** in (b) and (c) does not make their cases identical.

**Se mann gedǣlde ðā fuglas fram ðǣm dēore.** — The man separated the birds from the animal. **Ðā fuglas** is A plural, the direct object; **ðǣm dēore** is D neuter singular after **fram**. Keep the supplied **gedǣlde**. The plural birds and singular animal retain their separate numbers.
Work in the following order. A supplied pronunciation for a particular word or form takes precedence over a general pattern.

For the rules below, the **back-vowel spellings** are **a/ā, o/ō, u/ū**. The relevant **front-vowel spellings** are **e/ē, i/ī, æ/ǣ**; the diphthongs **ea/ēa, eo/ēo, ie/īe** also begin at the front of the mouth. Although **y/ȳ** are front vowels in articulation, their spelling is not a reliable instruction to give **c** or **g** a front sound. Use the supplied pronunciation in such words.
| e/ē, i/ī, æ/ǣ, or a front diphthong | **ch** as in *chin* | **cealf**, “calf”, begins with **ch**. |

These are useful defaults, with lexical exceptions. **Cēlan**, “cool”, begins with **k** despite **ē**. Both **c** letters in **cyrice**, “church”, are **ch**: learn its initial sound with the word, rather than deducing it from **y**. Keep all three syllables, including the final **e**.

Compare **dīc**, “ditch; dike”, with **dīcas**, “ditches; dikes”. Final **c** after **ī** has **ch**; before the **a** of the longer form it has **k**. An ending can therefore change the consonant sound. In other positions **k** is the ordinary starting point, but some words need a supplied pronunciation. Do not extend the after-**i/ī** rule to every front vowel.
Learn **sēcan**, “seek”, as a supplied exception: its **c** is **ch** as in *chin*, despite the following **a**. The back-vowel pattern does not override a word's stated pronunciation.

Otherwise use the non-**y** branch below, unless a word has a supplied exceptional pronunciation. At the beginning, a consonant between **g** and a later front vowel prevents the first row from applying: look at the immediate neighbour. The **g** rule after a front vowel is broader than the **c** rule after **i/ī**; keep them distinct. The earlier caution about **y/ȳ** still applies.
**5. For non-y g, decide between stopped and continuous g.**

For the continuous **g**, put the back of the tongue near the position for hard **g**, but leave a narrow gap. Let air pass continuously while the throat vibrates: the sound can be held, unlike the stopped **g** of *go*. Its phonetic sign is **[ɣ]**. Do not omit it or substitute **y**. First selecting the **y** or non-**y** branch prevents this rule from changing the final sound of **dæg** into continuous **g**.

The main stress normally falls on the first syllable, as in **habban**, “have”. Prefixes complicate this: **ge-** is unstressed, **be-** and **for-** usually are, and a prefixed verb generally stresses its root. When **ge-** precedes a one-syllable root, the word has two syllables and the root receives the stress. A supplied division identifies the prefix where needed. A macron indicates duration regardless of which syllable is stressed.

**A2.** **węnde**, “went”; **wēnde**, “thought; supposed”. Explain the vowel contrast. Does the hook under **ę** require a sound different from ordinary short **e**? Keep the final **e** audible in both words.
**B2.** **c** in **micel**, “large; great”, and **micles**, “large; great” (a declined form). Do the two forms have the same consonant sound? Explain from the immediate neighbours of **c**.

**B8.** **sc** in **scūfan**, “thrust”, and **cw** in **cwæð**, “said”. Decide whether each spelling gives one consonant sound or a sequence. Does the back vowel **ū** require a separate **k** in the first word?

**C6.** Compare **ð** in **hǣlðu**, “health”, with **f** in **ǣfre**, “ever; always”. The unvoiced **th** in **hǣlðu** is supplied lexical information from §5. Explain why that fact takes precedence over the ordinary between-voiced-sounds rule, while the ordinary rule applies to **ǣfre**. This is an exception comparison, not a request to deduce the exception from its spelling.
**D1.** **sittan**, “sit”. Does prolonging **tt** lengthen **i**, or add a syllable?
**D3.** **gewrit**, “letter; written document”; division **ge-writ**. Apply the prefix rule to stress, and pronounce both **w** and **r** without inserting another vowel.
**D4.** **forlǣtan**, “abandon; forsake”; division **for-lǣtan**. This is a prefixed verb. Locate its stress from the prefix rule, and explain what the macron tells you separately.

inspected_context_lines.text: The verb has the division **ge-scēop**, with prefix **ge-**. The sentence's meaning and grammatical forms are supplied; apply the pronunciation rules to read it aloud, then answer these sound questions.

4. Fulk §§16,18,135a–d, pp.11–13,103–104 / PDF23–25,115–116; Cook §§7,10, pp.8–9 / PDF24–25. **Cealf, dīc, dīcas** follow Fulk §135b, with his pronunciation overpoints omitted; Cook's vocabulary, p.283 / PDF299, also gives **dīc**. For **sēcan**, Cook's vocabulary, p.311 / PDF327, supplies the form and meaning as a headword variant; Fulk §135b supports the **ch** value with its explicitly prefixed infinitive example. The conditions for noninitial **c** are narrower than those for **g**. Earlier vowel changes, later endings and analogy explain some exceptions to the practical spelling patterns; the sound-history appendix treats these matters separately.

8. Adapted from Cook, Reader I, p.123 / PDF139, first prose line: remove **On anginne**, move **God** before the verb, and omit the three apparatus cues. The retained words are not respelled. The original sentence and notes remain in the source transcription. The full meaning and grammatical forms are supplied here; the sound questions apply the guide's rules. The separate **ge-scēop** division identifies a prefix and does not respell the reading.

9. The new practice forms are checked against Fulk §§16–24,135, pp.11–15,103–104 / PDF23–27,115–116; Cook §§4–5,53,121, pp.6–7,37,74 / PDF22–23,53,90, Reader I p.123 / PDF139, and vocabulary pp.283,288–289,296,309–312 / PDF299,304–305,312,325–328. **Hȳdan** is printed in Cook, *Exercises in Old English*, V.18.9, p.9 / PDF17; the original exercise is unchanged. “Thought; supposed” modernizes Cook's gloss “weened” for **wēnde**. Dictionary division hyphens in **gewrit** and **forlǣtan** are omitted, as elsewhere in the course; their separate practice divisions identify the prefixes.

**A2. węnde, “went”; wēnde, “thought; supposed”.** Short **ę** has the vowel of *bet*. Long **ē** has the steady initial vowel of *day*, held without the glide. The hook adds no separate sound. Both words have two syllables, with an audible light **e** in the second.

**B1. cēosað, “choose”.** Initial **c** is **ch**, as in *chin*, before the front diphthong **ēo**. This vetted example follows the ordinary initial pattern. The following diphthong remains one long glide.

**B2. micel, “large; great”; micles, a declined form.** In **micel**, **c** is **ch**: it follows **i** and precedes **e**. In **micles**, it is **k**: it immediately precedes the consonant **l**. The same word can change its consonant sound when the form changes. Merely noticing the preceding **i** misses the second condition.

**B4. fæger, “beautiful; fair”; regn, “rain”.** Both have **g** pronounced as **y** in *yes*. It follows a front vowel, **æ** or **e**, and no back vowel immediately follows it. In **regn**, **g** comes before **n**, not after it; the stopped-**g** condition “after **n**” therefore does not apply. Do not transfer the **c**-before-consonant rule to **g**.

**B6. brycg, “bridge”; singan, “sing”.** **Cg** has the final consonant sound of *bridge*. **Ng** has the sequence heard in *finger*, including the stopped **g**; do not reduce it to the end of modern English *sing*. The short **y** of **brycg** uses the tongue position of *bit* with rounded lips. Combination rules take priority over single-letter rules.

**B8. scūfan, “thrust”; cwæð, “said”.** **Sc** gives the single **sh** sound of *ship*, even before **ū**. **Cw** gives **k** followed by **w**, joined without an inserted vowel. Applying a single-**c** rule inside **sc** would wrongly produce a separate **k**.

**C6. hǣlðu, “health”; ǣfre, “ever; always”.** The supplied exception gives **ð** in **hǣlðu** unvoiced **th**, although **l** and **u** are voiced. In **ǣfre**, the ordinary rule gives voiced **f** between **ǣ** and **r**. A word-specific pronunciation takes priority over the default. Recognizing that limit is the task; deriving the exceptional sound from visible spelling is not required.

**D2. sunne, “sun”.** Two syllables, with stress on the first. Hold medial **nn** longer, as with the **n** across *pen-knife*. Its duration adds no syllable. Keep the final light **e** audible; modern English's one-syllable *sun* is not the model for the whole word.

**D3. gewrit, “letter; written document”.** Two syllables; stress **writ**, after unstressed **ge-**. Pronounce **w+r** without an inserted vowel. There is no doubled consonant. The vowel **i** remains short despite receiving the stress.

**D4. forlǣtan, “abandon; forsake”.** Three syllables, with stress on **lǣ** in the root. The supplied division identifies unstressed **for-**. The macron says that **ǣ** is long; the prefix/root rule determines stress. There is no doubled consonant, and final **-tan** remains audible.
